newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan watchdog proposes that ministry punish Nomura.
newsitem.headline: Japan watchdog proposes that ministry punish Nomura.

text.p: Japan's top securities watchdog on Tuesday proposed that the finance minister impose penalties against embattled Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

The long-awaited recommendation by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) will pave the way for the Finance Ministry (MOF) to take action against Nomura, expected to include the suspension of some of the top brokerage's key businesses, within a month, industry sources said.

The penalties are expected to be the heaviest ever imposed by the MOF, as Tokyo prosecutors have already indicted Nomura itself, its former president Hideo Sakamaki and former managing director Nobutaka Fujikura for a second time on suspicion that they made illegal payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.
The high-profile scandal was revealed in March by Nomura itself and has also led to the arrest of 11 current and former officials from Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.

After the SESC made the recommendation, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a group of reporters that his ministry will administer strict penalties against Nomura after it discusses the SESC recommendations with the brokerage.
Mitsuzuka said his ministry would decide on the punishment for the scandal-hit brokerage after scrutinising legal precedents and the details of the recommendation.

The securities watchdog said it proposed that the finance minister punish Nomura Securities because the company itself and four of its executives, including the former president, apparently violated Japan's securities law by compensating clients for investment losses.

Nomura contributed around 47.5 million yen ($416,000) worth of profits earned from discretionary deals to a client over the January to June period in 1995, which involved transferring money on five occasions from a Nomura account to the corporate client's account, it said.
In March 1995, Nomura paid about 2.2 million yen ($19,200) of profits raised through warrant trading to the client, it said.

An SESC official told reporters that the watchdog also recommended that the finance minister take appropriate measures to improve Nomura's internal risk control system to avoid any recurrence of the activities. Five departments in Nomura were involved in the company's attempts to hide the illegal payoffs.
It was the first time the watchdog has made a proposal about a brokerage's internal control system.

The illegal compensation for the client happened even though the top brokerage established a system to prevent such illegal deals after it was involved in a similar scandal for compensating a client for losses in 1991, he said.
Meanwhile, Tokyo Stock Exchange president Mitsuhide Yamaguchi said there may be an impact on the stock market if the brokerage's operations are restricted.

Industry sources said that the stock market has largely digested the impact of the expected penalties against Nomura as clients have already defected from the giant brokerage and it has also been suspended from underwriting government bonds.

However, the market was concerned about the range and the length of the penalties against Nomura. "If they are much harsher than we had expected, then market sentiment may be hurt," said one analyst. ($1=114 yen)
